messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Thorne, of African descent, was twenty-five when he sat in the clinic chair, but the narrative of his present began three years prior, on a rain-slicked street outside the precinct. Officers moved to detain a man nearby, and the heavy thud of boots on wet asphalt, the crackle of a police radio, and a familiar pop song drifting from a passing car’s window converged into a single, sharp moment. Marcus had come to believe that the pavement itself could betray him, that danger did not announce itself but arrived as an immediate presence. In the months that followed, his memories of that stretch of concrete felt more real and vivid than any of his ordinary recollections. When he closed his eyes, he sometimes heard the exact rhythm of the boots and the distant chorus of that song playing inside his head. He tried to explain the night to his partner and colleagues, but he was certain that the words slipped away; he would lose the thread before he could finish, as if the story was too heavy to hold together. As a journalist, Marcus spent his days navigating newsrooms, press conferences, and assignment desks, yet the city had slowly transformed into a field of parallel alerts. He began wearing oversized sweaters and high-collared coats to conceal his clothing and avoid being noticed by passing officers. When he walked to file copy at the downtown bureau, the rhythmic clip of footsteps behind him made him pause, his shoulders tightening until he turned to check if someone was following. Certain songs—particularly the ones with steady, percussive beats—would halt him mid-sentence, pulling his attention to the exact frequency of the night he was stopped. He avoided grief reminders wherever they surfaced: a dropped photograph, a closed café, a colleague’s quiet mourning felt too close to the edge. He had come to believe that feeling anything at all, whether sorrow or joy, remained a distinct burden. When a producer asked him to cover a new district across town, he declined, avoiding unfamiliar places while he could not assess the danger. His concentration frayed alongside these habits; he would sit in the corner of rooms, watching the doors and the ceiling as much as the documents on his desk. The years did not pass so much as accumulate around him. What frightened him most was not the incident itself, but the quiet certainty that his life had been destroyed by it. The editorials he used to write with ease now sat half-finished; the long walks through Central Park, the weekend dinners, the late-night phone calls—all of it felt beyond his grasp. He was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him, and the world felt permanently calibrated to his alarm. His relationship remained, but his avoidance had grown into a steady routine: he stayed close to familiar routes, kept his voice low, and let conversations circle the edges of the incident without ever landing on it. He had come to believe that he used to be a happy person, but now he was always miserable. The absence of good days coexisted with his daily routine; the persistent background hum of vigilance simply occupied the same hours as his work, his sleep, and his conversations, making ordinary days feel like holding breath. He finally walked into the clinic on a Tuesday, drawn by a colleague’s quiet suggestion and the slow erosion of his own schedule. His PCL-5 scores settled at seventy-six, a number that mirrored the weight he carried. The clinic doors felt familiar enough, but he still checked the sidewalk behind him before stepping inside. In his chair, Marcus spoke of the footsteps, the songs, the way his memories pressed against his ribs like living things. He was not looking for a cure so much as for a way to step out of the periphery without losing himself. He feared the moment when the familiar would turn unfamiliar again, when the next bootfall or song would pull him back to that pavement. Yet, as he sat there, watching the light move across the floor, he hoped simply to reclaim the capacity to move through his own life without bracing for what was behind him.
